always plan an escape route before entering a place

Threat.value: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard

issues.item: Compulsive Cleaning: I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control
issues.explanation: Compulsive cleaning is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The threat items describe hypervigilance and safety-positioning in response to interpersonal danger, but no other item suggests contamination, orderliness, or a ritualised control theme. As a maladaptive strategy, it feels disconnected from the threat pattern represented here.

issues.item: Memory Detachment: I detach myself from the memories
issues.explanation: The formulation has Threat strongly linked with Maladaptive Strategies, while Memory is isolated with no active edges. The maladaptive strategy items should therefore be tightly connected to current threat management. 'Memory Detachment' is a memory-focused coping response that implies an active Memory-related process, which is not reflected elsewhere and does not align with the specified edge pattern. In contrast, reassurance seeking, hypervigilance towards people, and the threat items form a coherent threat-management cluster for captivity trauma.

vignette: When Marae, a 53‑year‑old Samoan photographer, was nineteen, he was captured during a protest in Wellington and held for three months in a deserted warehouse. The walls were damp, the lights flickered, and every creak of the floorboards felt like a threat. He remembers the smell of wet concrete and the cold, damp air seeping through the cracks, and he remembers the sudden, almost imperceptible movement of a guard’s shadow across the room. Those movements felt like an imminent attack; the sense that danger could erupt at any moment was all-consuming. After he was freed, Marae carried that sense of danger with him into his daily life. The first time he left his apartment, he paused at the street corner, feeling a sudden jolt of anxiety as a cyclist swerved too close. He immediately chose the curb that felt most protected, stepping into it as if it were a safe haven. That tiny decision – always picking the “safe seat” – became a habit; he now always looks for the corner of a room or the back seat of a car where he feels most shielded, believing that sitting in a more secure spot will prevent a sudden threat from materializing. In the weeks after the escape, Marae’s body stayed tense. He carried a constant readiness, as if a hidden trigger could snap his calm into panic. When a friend laughed loudly, he felt his muscles tighten, his heart rate spike, and his mind race through the possibility that someone might suddenly appear to snatch his camera and run. His hands trembled when he tried to focus the lens; the sight of a moving crowd made him flinch as if the nearest person could turn into a weapon. In the studio, he now places his tripod on the far side of the table, arranging the camera so it’s easy to get out of the way if someone suddenly rushes toward him. The act of planning an escape route before entering a place has become part of his routine, a way to feel in control of a future threat that might arise. Marae’s need for reassurance grew alongside his constant vigilance. Whenever he is unsure whether a situation is truly safe, he will ask a colleague or his wife, Leilani, “Are you sure that’s okay?” He feels that unless someone else confirms it, the danger might be imminent. This reassurance seeking feeds his hypervigilance: the more he hears that something might be wrong, the more he interprets every movement as a possible threat. When Leilani says, “Everything’s fine,” he still watches the door frame for a second, as if it might open unexpectedly. He has learned that the only way to soothe the body’s tension is to hear that others think the environment is safe, so the reassurance process becomes a cycle that keeps the threat perception heightened. The camera has become a symbol of his fear. On shoots, Marae insists on having a plan of where he can drop his equipment or leave the site if he feels the room’s atmosphere shift. He tells his crew to be alert, but his own alertness dominates the session. He keeps his focus on the camera’s manual, double‑checking that the flash isn’t ready to go off in a moment that feels too sudden. When a sudden sound from the audience jolts him, he scrambles to find a place to hide his gear. He avoids crowds and large events, preferring to work with small groups or in quiet studios. Each avoidance strengthens his belief that large gatherings are inherently dangerous, reinforcing the cycle of threat perception and protective behaviors. The impact on his marriage is subtle but palpable. Leilani has learned to give him reassurance without being asked, but she also worries about the time he spends planning exits. Their conversations often shift to safety protocols, and Marae can feel the strain when he tells Leilani that the living room’s couch feels unsafe compared to the dining table. The couple's intimacy has been affected; Marae feels he must always be on guard even in his own home, which creates distance. After several months of declining performance at his photography agency—missed deadlines because he left early from shoots, increased tension during client meetings—Marae finally sat down with Leilani and said, “I’m scared that I’m going to have a panic attack right in front of my clients, and I can’t keep doing this.” He expressed that the fear of an unknown threat keeps him from being present, from enjoying his art, and from spending time with his family. That night, after watching the city’s lights from their balcony, he realized he could no longer ignore the loop of fear and vigilance that had become his reality. He is now hoping for relief from the constant body tension, and he fears that without help he will continue to lose the very life he loves—his work, his home, his connection to Leilani.
